detailed_rationale:
REC is a quasi-sovereign power-and-infrastructure NBFC (Navratna PSU) with a loan book at an all-time high of Rs5.84 lakh crore as of 31-Mar-2026, of which the renewable-energy book has grown to Rs75,347 crore (+30% YoY) - a genuine and welcome diversification away from legacy thermal/discom exposure, though it still remains only ~13% of the total book. FY26 headline profit of Rs16,282 crore was the company's highest ever, and the balance-sheet metrics that matter for a power financier look genuinely clean: net Stage-3 (NNPA) at just 0.12%, gross Stage-3 down to ~1.06% (Sep-2025), Stage-2 loans down 75% YoY, and net credit-impaired assets falling to 0.20% from 0.74% over 9M FY26. But two things sit underneath that headline that a fundamental read cannot skip. First, growth quality: management reaffirmed an 11-12% loan-growth target for FY26, but actual net AUM growth came in at only ~3% YoY (roughly Rs17,000 crore added on a ~Rs5.67 lakh crore base) because ~Rs49,000 crore of prepayments - state discoms/generators refinancing away from REC, likely toward cheaper bank/bond funding as their own credit has improved - ate into gross disbursements. Q4 FY26 alone saw disbursements down 9% QoQ. That is a legitimate signal that REC's role as marginal financier-of-last-resort to the power sector is shrinking as sector credit conditions normalize, not just a one-quarter blip. Second, earnings quality: REC's dramatic asset-quality improvement over the past two years has been substantially a function of large stressed-asset resolutions (four legacy thermal projects resolved with recoveries above provisioned levels; e.g. Bhadreshwar Vidyut - Rs709.78 crore written off against an IBC resolution plan with a Rs59.54 crore ECL provision reversal in Q3 FY26) rather than pure organic seasoning. That is precisely why the standalone impairment charge collapsed to Rs201.22 crore in FY26 from Rs1,019.41 crore in FY25 - a huge one-off tailwind to reported PAT. Q4 FY26 is the first quarter that tailwind visibly faded: standalone net profit fell ~21% YoY and ~17% QoQ to Rs3,362 crore as the company rebuilt provisions more conservatively (Macquarie's phrase), NIM came in soft at 3.55% for the quarter (3.43%/2.62% spread for the full year), and a widening 'other comprehensive loss' from FX-hedging fair-value movements (Rs3,046.83 crore standalone in Q4 vs Rs1,050.14 crore a year earlier) dragged total comprehensive income for the quarter down to just Rs315.47 crore. None of this hits reported PAT directly, but it is a real, non-trivial economic cost of REC's offshore-borrowing/hedging book that headline PAT growth understates.

The overhanging event for the next 9-12 months is the PFC-REC merger, not incremental operating performance. PFC has been REC's promoter since March 2019 (52.63% stake, acquired for ~Rs14,500 crore/Rs139.50 per share), and on 28-Jun-2026 both boards approved a scheme to fold REC into PFC at an 88:100 share swap ratio (88 PFC shares for every 100 REC shares). Using the announced ratio, REC's implied value (PFC price x 0.88) worked out to roughly a 4% premium to REC's prevailing market price at announcement, narrowing to ~2.3% shortly after as the two stocks re-priced - a modest but not punitive outcome for REC minority holders on the terms as struck, though the 'premium' is not locked in: it moves with PFC's share price between now and completion, and PFC (as REC's own majority owner) had an inherent role in commissioning the 'independent' valuation that set it. The approval process is still at an early stage - shareholder/creditor meetings, stock-exchange no-objections, SEBI, and NCLT sanction are all outstanding, with an MCA filing expected from August 2026, an NCLT chairperson's report targeted for December 2026, and a targeted effective date of 1-Apr-2027. Until then REC continues to trade, report results, and pay dividends as a standalone listed entity, but the whole thesis for a fresh three-to-five-year view has to acknowledge that 'RECLTD' the listed entity is scheduled to disappear inside that window, replaced by a bigger, more thermal-weighted combined PFC-REC book whose capital-allocation and governance will no longer be REC's own board's to decide.

On valuation: at a CMP of roughly Rs349-352 (mid-July 2026, market cap ~Rs92,400-92,800 crore), REC trades at a P/B of ~1.11-1.18x against a trailing consolidated ROE of ~20% (sources range 19.9-21.5%), a trailing P/E of ~5.4x, and a dividend yield of ~5.3-5.6% (FY26 total dividend Rs18.55/share). Running a simple Gordon-growth justified-P/B check (P/B = (ROE-g)/(CoE-g)) on the trailing 20% ROE with a normal-for-the-credit-profile cost of equity of ~13-14% shows the current 1.11-1.18x multiple would be justified even by very modest or flat forward growth - i.e., on pure trailing numbers the stock screens statistically cheap. But that trailing 20% ROE is inflated by the fading resolution-write-back tailwind described above; a more sustainable, normalized ROE once credit costs revert toward a 'through-cycle' level is more plausibly in the mid-to-high teens. Rerunning the same math on a normalized ~16-17% ROE still implies a fair P/B modestly above where the stock trades today, which reads as the market applying either a higher implicit cost of equity (merger/integration uncertainty, thermal-legacy memory, government-linked-entity discount) or its own skepticism about growth (the 3% actual AUM growth vs 11-12% guided). Net: REC is not expensive on any reasonable normalized-earnings view, but it is also not a name to build fresh high-conviction upside around, given the growth-quality and merger-completion uncertainty sitting on top of an otherwise clean balance sheet.
recommendation_rationale: Hold rather than Sell because there is no acute deterioration to point to - asset quality is genuinely improving (NNPA 0.12%, Stage-2 down 75% YoY), the spread/NIM franchise is stable (~2.62% spread), the dividend yield (~5.3-5.6%) provides real income support, and reverse-DCF math does not show the stock priced above what even a normalized (not peak) ROE can justify. Hold rather than a more constructive call because the headline 'record profit' growth story is significantly a fading one-off (stressed-asset write-backs, now normalizing upward in Q4), net loan growth is running at ~3% against an 11-12% target due to heavy prepayments, OCI/hedging volatility is a real if non-headline earnings drag, and the pending PFC merger removes REC as a standalone entity within the next 9-12 months with terms that are only modestly favorable on paper and not fixed until completion. That combination argues for neutral, not a directional call.
summary: REC is a government-backed power and infrastructure lender with genuinely clean asset quality today (bad loans near zero) and a fast-growing renewable-energy book, and it pays a high dividend (over 5% yield) at a low earnings multiple. But look past the FY26 'highest-ever profit' headline and two things stand out: actual loan-book growth was only about 3% (well below the 11-12% management had targeted) because a wave of borrowers prepaid and refinanced elsewhere, and a large chunk of the recent profit improvement came from one-off recoveries on old stressed power loans - a tailwind that visibly faded in the March-2026 quarter, when profit fell 21% year-on-year. On top of that, REC is set to merge into its parent, Power Finance Corporation, some time around April 2027, on terms (88 PFC shares for every 100 REC shares) that look roughly fair but are not locked in and remove REC as an independent, dividend-paying, renewables-tilted investment on its own terms. We rate this a Hold: the balance sheet and yield support the stock, but the growth-quality question and the pending merger overhang keep us from being more constructive.
positive_para: REC's core lending franchise to India's power sector remains fundamentally sound: net Stage-3 (bad loan) ratio of just 0.12%, Stage-2 (early-warning) loans down 75% year-on-year, and net credit-impaired assets down to 0.20% from 0.74% over nine months of FY26 - a genuinely improving risk profile, not just a cosmetic one, aided by real recoveries on legacy stressed thermal-power exposures. The renewable-energy loan book has grown to Rs75,347 crore (+30% YoY), giving REC a credible, growing exposure to India's energy-transition capex cycle rather than pure legacy thermal/discom risk. The spread (2.62%) and NIM (3.43% full-year) franchise is stable, the stock is cheap on trailing multiples (P/B ~1.1-1.2x, P/E ~5.4x for a ~20% trailing ROE business), and the dividend yield of ~5.3-5.6% (Rs18.55/share paid for FY26) provides a real income cushion. Sell-side coverage (Macquarie, Morgan Stanley) stayed constructive even after the Q4 miss, both citing valuation support - a signal that institutional confidence in the core franchise has not broken.
negative_para: The strongest bear point is that REC's recent earnings quality has leaned heavily on a fading tailwind: the collapse in standalone impairment charges (Rs201.22 crore in FY26 versus Rs1,019.41 crore in FY25) reflects large one-off stressed-asset resolution write-backs, not a structurally lower steady-state credit cost - and Q4 FY26 is the first quarter where that reverses, with 'conservative' re-provisioning (Macquarie's characterization) driving a 21% YoY, 17% QoQ profit decline and NIM softening to 3.55%. Layered on top, actual net loan-book growth of ~3% YoY badly lagged the 11-12% guided target because ~Rs49,000 crore of borrower prepayments (states/discoms refinancing away from REC) offset gross disbursements - a real signal that REC's addressable, price-setting role in power financing is narrowing as competing capital gets cheaper and more available to its traditional borrowers. A widening FX-hedging-driven other-comprehensive-loss (Rs3,046.83 crore standalone in Q4, versus Rs1,050.14 crore a year prior) is a further, non-headline earnings-quality flag. And REC will not exist as an independent listed entity for much longer: it is being merged into promoter PFC (which already holds 52.63% of REC) at an 88:100 swap ratio that implied only a modest ~2-4% premium at announcement and is not fixed until the NCLT-sanctioned close (targeted 1-Apr-2027) - a nine-to-twelve-month period of integration, governance, and terms-drift risk during which REC minority holders have no real say beyond the shareholder vote on an already-negotiated ratio.
reverse_dcf_judgment: At CMP ~Rs349-352 (P/B ~1.11-1.18x, trailing consolidated ROE ~20%, P/E ~5.4x), a Gordon-growth justified-P/B check using the trailing ROE and a ~13-14% cost of equity shows the current multiple would be supported even by flat-to-modest forward growth - i.e., on unadjusted trailing numbers REC screens statistically cheap. But that ~20% trailing ROE is inflated by one-off stressed-asset resolution write-backs that visibly faded in Q4 FY26 (standalone impairment charges are already normalizing back up); a more sustainable, through-cycle ROE is more plausibly in the mid-to-high teens. Re-running the same math on a normalized ~16-17% ROE with ~6-8% growth (consistent with the ~3% actual AUM growth this year against an unmet 11-12% target) still implies a fair P/B modestly above the current level - the stock is not expensive even on a de-risked earnings view, but nor is it priced to reward fresh conviction, especially with the PFC merger removing REC as an independent compounding vehicle within the reverse-DCF's own multi-year horizon.
